title: Vector Spaces and Subspaces
description: Span, independence, basis and dimension; the four fundamental subspaces of a matrix; rank; and change of basis.
overview: The previous chapter treated vectors and matrices as arrays of numbers and gave rules for computing with them. This chapter explains what they mean. The set of all outputs of a linear model, the directions in which a model cannot distinguish inputs, the number of independent features in a data set, and the ways a coordinate system can be changed are all described by vector spaces and subspaces.

The central objects are the four fundamental subspaces of a matrix, whose dimensions are tied together by the rank. These explain when Ax = b has solutions, why XᵀX can be singular, and how PCA and the SVD work.
objectives: Define a subspace, the span of a set of vectors, linear independence, a basis and the dimension.
Find the rank, a basis for the column space and a basis for the null space of a matrix.
State and use the rank–nullity theorem and describe the four fundamental subspaces.
Describe the solution set of Ax = b as a particular solution plus the null space.
Change the basis and express a linear map in a new basis.

sections.title: Subspaces and span
body: Start with a picture. Stand at the origin of 3D space with two directions you are allowed to walk along, say east and north. By walking any amount along each (including backward), you can reach every point on the flat ground, but never a point above it. The ground is the set of everything reachable from those two directions, and it is a plane through the origin. A subspace is exactly this kind of set: closed under walking more or less along its directions and combining them. A **vector space** is a set of objects that can be added and multiplied by scalars, with the usual rules of arithmetic. ℝⁿ is the basic example; the polynomials of degree at most d and the continuous functions on an interval are others. A **subspace** is a subset of a vector space that is itself a vector space: it contains 0 and is closed under addition and scalar multiplication. In ℝ³ the subspaces are the origin, the lines through the origin, the planes through the origin, and ℝ³ itself.

The **span** of vectors v₁, …, v_k is the set of all their linear combinations, c₁v₁ + … + c_kv_k. It is the smallest subspace that contains them. The span of one non-zero vector is a line, and of two vectors that do not lie on a common line is a plane.

example.title: Is a vector in a span?
example.problem: Is b = (3, 5, 7) in the span of v₁ = (1, 1, 1) and v₂ = (0, 2, 4)?
example.solution: We need c₁v₁ + c₂v₂ = b: c₁ = 3 (first coordinate), c₁ + 2c₂ = 5 gives c₂ = 1, and then the third coordinate c₁ + 4c₂ = 7 ✓. Yes: b = 3v₁ + v₂.

list: The set of all points with x + y + z = 0 is a subspace of ℝ³ (a plane through the origin). The set x + y + z = 1 is not (it does not contain 0).

The predictions Xθ of a linear model, as θ ranges over all weights, form the span of the columns of X. A linear model can only predict vectors in this subspace; least squares projects the targets onto it.

check.q: Which is a subspace of ℝ²?

sections.title: Independence, basis and dimension
body: Vectors v₁, …, v_k are **linearly independent** if the only combination giving zero is the trivial one: c₁v₁ + … + c_kv_k = 0 implies every c_i = 0. Otherwise they are **dependent**: at least one of them is a combination of the others and carries no new information. Putting the vectors in the columns of a matrix A, they are independent exactly when Ax = 0 has only the solution x = 0.

A **basis** of a subspace is a set of independent vectors that span it. Every vector in the subspace is then a //unique// combination of the basis vectors, and the coefficients are its **coordinates**. All bases of a subspace have the same number of vectors, and this number is the **dimension**. The standard basis e₁, …, e_n has dimension n for ℝⁿ.

example.title: A dependent set
example.solution: v₃ = v₁ + v₂, so v₁ + v₂ − v₃ = 0 is a nontrivial combination: they are dependent. They span only a plane (dimension 2), spanned by v₁ and v₂, which form a basis of it.

list: More than n vectors in ℝⁿ are always dependent. Fewer than n vectors cannot span ℝⁿ.
The polynomials of degree ≤ 2 form a 3-dimensional space with basis 1, x, x². The coordinates of 4 − 3x + x² are (4, −3, 1).

A feature that is a linear combination of the others (for example weight in kg and weight in lb) makes the columns of the data matrix dependent. Then XᵀX is singular and the weights are not uniquely determined.

check.q: How many vectors can a linearly independent set in ℝ⁴ have, at most?

sections.title: Rank and the four fundamental subspaces
body: Think of the matrix A as a machine that turns an input vector with n entries into an output vector with m entries. Two questions describe what the machine does. Which outputs can it produce at all? That set is the column space. Which inputs does it destroy, mapping them to zero? That set is the null space. The row space and left null space are the same two questions asked about Aᵀ. Every m × n matrix A has four subspaces attached to it.

body: The number r is the **rank** of A: the number of pivots after elimination, which equals the dimension of the column space and the dimension of the row space (the column rank equals the row rank). The dimensions of the column space and null space add up to the number of columns:

This is the **rank–nullity theorem**. The free variables (columns without pivots) number n − r, and each yields one basis vector of the null space. The pivot columns of A form a basis of the column space.

example.title: All four subspaces of a 3 × 4 matrix
example.problem: Find the rank and a basis for the column space and the null space of A = [[1, 2, 0, 1], [2, 4, 1, 4], [3, 6, 1, 5]].
solution: Eliminate: R₂ − 2R₁ = (0, 0, 1, 2); R₃ − 3R₁ = (0, 0, 1, 2); then R₃ − R₂ = 0. The pivots are in columns 1 and 3, so the rank is r = 2. The reduced form has rows (1, 2, 0, 1) and (0, 0, 1, 2).
Column space: the pivot columns (1, 2, 3) and (0, 1, 1). Indeed column 2 = 2 · column 1, and column 4 = column 1 + 2 · column 3.

Null space: the free variables are x₂ and x₄, and x₁ = −2x₂ − x₄ and x₃ = −2x₄. Setting (x₂, x₄) = (1, 0) and (0, 1) gives the basis (−2, 1, 0, 0) and (−1, 0, −2, 1). The dimension is 2 = n − r = 4 − 2 ✓.
The left null space has dimension m − r = 1, and the row space has dimension 2.

body.tip: Rank in practice: the numerical rank of a matrix is the number of singular values above a small tolerance (see the SVD chapter). Computing rank by exact elimination is unreliable in floating point.

sections.title: When is Ax = b solvable?
body: The system Ax = b has a solution if and only if b is in the column space of A. When it does, the complete set of solutions is a particular solution plus any vector in the null space:

body.eq: x = x_p + x_n,    A x_p = b,   A x_n = 0

body: So the solution is unique exactly when N(A) = {0}, i.e. when A has full column rank r = n (independent columns).

example.title: Complete solution
example.problem: For the 3 × 4 matrix of the previous example, solve Ax = (1, 3, 4).
example.solution: The vector b = (1, 3, 4) = column 1 + column 3, so it is in the column space, and a particular solution is x_p = (1, 0, 1, 0). Adding the null space gives all solutions: x = (1, 0, 1, 0) + s(−2, 1, 0, 0) + t(−1, 0, −2, 1) for any s and t. For b = (1, 0, 0), which is not a combination of the columns, there is no solution.

body: **Multicollinearity** (dependent or nearly dependent columns of X) makes N(X) non-trivial or nearly so. Then XᵀX is singular or ill-conditioned: coefficients are not identifiable, and small changes in the data produce large changes in the fit. Ridge regression repairs this by adding λI. A data matrix with low rank, such as many users' ratings driven by a few tastes, is the premise of matrix factorization and PCA.

sections.title: Change of basis
body: A vector is an arrow, and its coordinates are a description of the arrow in some language. Using east and north as the reference directions, the arrow (3, 1) means "3 east, 1 north." Using northeast and northwest instead, the same arrow gets different numbers. Changing the basis changes the description, not the arrow, in the same way that translating a sentence changes the words but not the meaning. A vector has coordinates only relative to a chosen basis. Let the columns of an invertible matrix P be a new basis b₁, …, b_n. If a vector has coordinates c in this basis, its standard coordinates are x = Pc, and conversely c = P⁻¹x.

A linear map that acts on standard coordinates as x ↦ Ax acts on coordinates in the new basis as c ↦ P⁻¹AP c. The matrices A and B = P⁻¹AP represent the same map in different bases and are called **similar**. They have the same determinant, trace, rank and eigenvalues. Choosing a basis in which B is as simple as possible is the idea behind diagonalization and the SVD.

example.title: A reflection made diagonal
example.problem: In ℝ², the reflection across the line y = x is x ↦ Ax with A = [[0, 1], [1, 0]]. Express it in the basis b₁ = (1, 1), b₂ = (1, −1), and find the coordinates of (3, 1) in this basis.
solution: The reflection fixes b₁ (it lies on the line): Ab₁ = b₁. It reverses b₂: Ab₂ = (−1, 1) = −b₂. In the new basis its matrix is B = diag(1, −1).

Coordinates of (3, 1): c₁(1, 1) + c₂(1, −1) = (3, 1) gives c₁ + c₂ = 3 and c₁ − c₂ = 1, so c = (2, 1). Reflecting multiplies the second coordinate by −1, giving (2, −1), which is 2(1, 1) − (1, −1) = (1, 3) in standard coordinates ✓.

list: The **image** (range) of a linear map is the column space of its matrix, and the **kernel** is the null space.

The simplest case is a diagonal B: the map just scales each basis vector. Not every matrix can be diagonalized, but every symmetric matrix can, by an orthonormal basis (the spectral theorem, next chapters).
Changing basis is how PCA works: it re-expresses the data in the basis of principal components, in which the covariance is diagonal.

check.q: Similar matrices A and P⁻¹AP always share
check.a: the same eigenvalues, determinant and trace

quiz.q: Which of these sets is a subspace of ℝ³?
quiz.why: The first is a plane through the origin, closed under addition and scaling. The set xyz = 0 is a union of three coordinate planes: (1, 1, 0) + (0, 0, 1) = (1, 1, 1) is not in it.

quiz.q: Which vector lies in the span of (1, 1, 0) and (0, 1, 1)?
quiz.why: c₁ = 2 from the first coordinate, c₁ + c₂ = 5 gives c₂ = 3, and the third coordinate equals c₂ = 3 ✓. The other vectors fail the third-coordinate check.

quiz.q: X is a 100 × 3 data matrix with independent columns. The set of all prediction vectors Xθ is
wrong: all of ℝ¹⁰⁰, one dimension per example
quiz.why: The predictions are combinations of the 3 columns, which live in ℝ¹⁰⁰, so they fill a 3-dimensional subspace. Most target vectors y lie outside it.

quiz.q: Which of these sets of vectors is linearly dependent?
quiz.why: (1, 2, 3) + (3, 4, 5) = (4, 6, 8) = 2(2, 3, 4), a nontrivial relation. In each other set the only combination equal to zero has all coefficients 0.

quiz.q: Using the basis 1, x, x² of the polynomials of degree at most 2, what are the coordinates of 2x² − 5?
quiz.why: The coordinates are the coefficients of 1, x and x² in that order: −5 for 1, 0 for x, and 2 for x².

quiz.q: Seven vectors are chosen in ℝ⁵. Which statement must be true?
wrong: At least two of them are zero vectors
quiz.why: No more than 5 vectors in ℝ⁵ can be independent. Seven vectors may still fail to span ℝ⁵, for example if all are multiples of one vector.

quiz.q: In a regression, the third feature column equals twice the first minus the second. What does this do to least squares?
quiz.a: Many different weight vectors achieve exactly the same minimal squared error
wrong: No weight vector reaches the minimum, so the error is unbounded
There is a unique solution, but its entries have large variance
The unique solution fits the training targets exactly
quiz.why: The columns are dependent, so X has a nontrivial null space, and adding any null-space vector to θ leaves Xθ unchanged. XᵀX is singular and the solution is not unique.

quiz.q: A 6 × 9 matrix has rank 4. What is the dimension of its left null space?
quiz.why: The left null space lives in ℝ⁶ and has dimension m − r = 6 − 4 = 2. The value 5 is the dimension of the null space, n − r.
R₂ − 2R₁ = (0, 0, 0, 1) and R₃ − 3R₁ = (0, 0, 0, 1), so R₃ − R₂ leaves a zero row. The pivots are in columns 1 and 4.

quiz.q: For A = [[1, 2, 1, 0], [2, 4, 2, 1], [3, 6, 3, 1]], which pair is a basis of the column space?
quiz.why: Take the columns of the original A in the pivot positions (1 and 4). Pivot columns of the reduced form are not in the column space, and the last option lists rows, which span the row space.

quiz.q: A has rows (1, 2, 2) and (2, 0, 1). Which vector is in its null space?
quiz.why: The rows give 2 + 6 − 8 = 0 and 4 − 4 = 0. A null-space vector is perpendicular to every row, so a row itself ((1, 2, 2)) or a multiple of one ((4, 0, 2)) cannot be in it.

quiz.q: For which right-hand side b is [[1, 2], [2, 4]]x = b solvable?
quiz.why: The column space is the line through (1, 2), so b must be a multiple of (1, 2). (5, 10) = 5(1, 2); the others are not proportional to (1, 2).

quiz.q: Suppose b ≠ 0, Ax = b has the solution (1, 0, 0), and N(A) is spanned by (1, −1, 2). Which vector also solves Ax = b?
quiz.why: (4, −3, 6) = (1, 0, 0) + 3(1, −1, 2) is a particular solution plus a null-space vector. (2, 0, 0) gives 2b, (1, −1, 2) gives 0, and (3, −1, 2) adds a vector outside the null space.

quiz.q: X is a 50 × 200 matrix of rank 50. For any target y, the equation Xθ = y has
quiz.a: infinitely many solutions, forming a 150-dimensional family
wrong: no solution in general, since y is a generic vector
infinitely many solutions, forming a 200-dimensional family
quiz.why: Rank 50 equals the number of rows, so the column space is all of ℝ⁵⁰ and every y is reachable. The null space has dimension 200 − 50 = 150, and that is the freedom in θ.

quiz.q: Why does Xθ = y usually have no exact solution when X is 100 × 5 with independent columns?
quiz.a: The column space is only 5-dimensional inside ℝ¹⁰⁰, and a typical y lies outside it
wrong: XᵀX is singular for tall matrices
X has more columns than rows
The null space of X is too large
quiz.why: A solution exists only if y is in the column space, which has dimension 5 in a 100-dimensional space. With independent columns the null space is trivial and XᵀX is invertible.

quiz.q: In the basis b₁ = (1, 1), b₂ = (1, 2), what are the coordinates of the vector (5, 8)?
quiz.why: Solve c₁ + c₂ = 5 and c₁ + 2c₂ = 8: c₂ = 3, c₁ = 2. The value (13, 21) arises from multiplying by P instead of P⁻¹.

quiz.q: A = [[2, 1], [0, 3]] acts on standard coordinates. What matrix represents the same map in the basis b₁ = (1, 0), b₂ = (1, 1)?
quiz.why: Ab₁ = (2, 0) = 2b₁ and Ab₂ = (3, 3) = 3b₂, so each basis vector is scaled and the new matrix is diagonal with entries 2 and 3, in the order of the basis.

quiz.q: Which class of matrices can always be diagonalized using an orthonormal basis?
wrong: All square matrices with positive entries
quiz.why: This is the spectral theorem. Invertible, triangular or positive matrices need not have a full set of eigenvectors, and even when they do the eigenvectors need not be orthogonal.

summary: A subspace contains 0 and is closed under addition and scaling. The span of vectors is the set of their linear combinations.
Vectors are independent if no one is a combination of the others. A basis is an independent spanning set; the number of vectors in it is the dimension.
An m × n matrix of rank r has column space and row space of dimension r, null space of dimension n − r and left null space of dimension m − r. Rank–nullity: r + dim N(A) = n.
Ax = b is solvable iff b is in the column space. The solutions are x_p + N(A), and unique iff the columns are independent. Collinear features make XᵀX singular.
Changing the basis replaces A by P⁻¹AP, which has the same eigenvalues. Choosing a good basis (such as eigenvectors or principal components) simplifies the map.

problems.q: Find the rank, a basis of the column space and the null space of A = [[1, 2, 3], [2, 4, 6], [1, 1, 2]].
problems.solution: R₂ − 2R₁ = 0 and R₃ − R₁ = (0, −1, −1). The pivots are in columns 1 and 2, so rank = 2. A basis of the column space is columns 1 and 2: (1, 2, 1) and (2, 4, 1). The free variable is x₃: from −x₂ − x₃ = 0 we get x₂ = −x₃, and from x₁ + 2x₂ + 3x₃ = 0, x₁ = −x₃. The null space is spanned by (−1, −1, 1), with dimension 1 = 3 − 2.
(7, 8, 9) = 2(4, 5, 6) − (1, 2, 3). So they are dependent. The rank of the matrix with these columns is 2.

problems.q: A data matrix X has 100 examples and 150 features, with rank 80. What are the dimensions of its column space and null space, and does Xθ = y have an exact solution for every y?
problems.solution: The column space has dimension 80 inside ℝ¹⁰⁰, and the null space has dimension 150 − 80 = 70. Since 80 < 100, the column space is not all of ℝ¹⁰⁰, so some y have no exact solution. For those in the column space there are infinitely many (a 70-dimensional family).
problems.a: 80 and 70; no, only y in the 80-dimensional column space.

problems.solution: Solve 2c₁ + c₂ = 5 and c₁ − c₂ = 1: adding gives 3c₁ = 6, c₁ = 2 and c₂ = 1. Check: 2(2, 1) + (1, −1) = (5, 1).

problems.q: Show that the null space of A is a subspace.
problems.solution: A0 = 0, so 0 is in N(A). If Ax = 0 and Ay = 0 then A(x + y) = Ax + Ay = 0 and A(cx) = cAx = 0. So N(A) is closed under addition and scaling.
problems.a: It contains 0 and is closed under addition and scalar multiplication.
